title: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — FIR registration and escalation
summary: The BNSS, 2023 (which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 from 1 July 2024) governs registration of information about cognizable offences (FIR) under Section 173, escalation when the SHO refuses, and Magistrates' powers to order investigation under Section 175.
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) — FIR and escalation pathway:

Section 173: every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, given orally or electronically to an officer in charge of a police station, must be reduced to writing, read over to the informant, and signed by the informant; a copy of the information must be furnished free of cost. The Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2014) 2 SCC 1 held (under the predecessor CrPC Section 154) that registration of an FIR is mandatory where the information discloses a cognizable offence — the principle carries to the BNSS regime.

Escalation if the station house officer refuses to register: (1) send the complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police, who may investigate or direct investigation (see BNSS Section 175 — verify the current subsection); (2) approach the concerned Judicial Magistrate, who may order investigation under Section 175(3); (3) file a private complaint before the Magistrate; (4) in appropriate cases, approach the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of mandamus.

Section 193 (replacing CrPC Section 200): examination of the complainant on oath in private complaints.

Preserve proof: carry a copy of the written complaint and dispatch receipts; demand the free FIR copy.

DEMO KNOWLEDGE BASE ENTRY — condensed summary for demonstration purposes. Section numbering under the new codes must be verified at indiacode.nic.in before relying on it.

title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — cheating and breach of trust
summary: The BNS, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 from 1 July 2024. Criminal breach of trust is now Section 316 (formerly IPC Section 406) and cheating is Section 318 (formerly IPC Section 420) — relevant to frauds, deposit misappropriation and scams.
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) — offences relevant to money and fraud disputes:

Section 316 — criminal breach of trust (replacing IPC Section 406): whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property or with dominion over it, dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to their own use, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of a legal contract or express direction, commits criminal breach of trust.

Section 318 — cheating (replacing IPC Section 420): whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces them to deliver property or to consent to retention of property, or intentionally induces them to do or omit to do anything they would not do if not so deceived, commits cheating. Online payment frauds, fake sellers and investment scams are prosecuted under this provision together with the Information Technology Act, 2000.

Related BNS provisions (verify numbering): forgery (formerly IPC 463-471), criminal intimidation (formerly IPC 503-506), and defamation as a civil-criminal matter.

A complaint to police/economic offences wing may cite these provisions where the facts disclose a cognizable offence; the complaint narrative should state facts chronologically rather than merely asserting legal conclusions.

title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — cybercrime provisions
summary: The IT Act, 2000 penalises unauthorized access and damage (Sections 43/66), identity theft (Section 66C) and cheating by personation using a computer resource (Section 66D) — the primary provisions for UPI frauds, phishing, hacking and online impersonation, reportable via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.
text:
Information Technology Act, 2000 — key cybercrime provisions:

Section 43 (civil liability) and Section 66 (criminal liability): unauthorized access to a computer, computer system or computer network; downloading/copying data without authorization; introducing viruses or damaging the system.

Section 66C — identity theft: fraudulent or dishonest use of the electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature of any other person. Punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine.

Section 66D — cheating by personation using a computer resource: cheating by any personation through communication device or computer resource, as is common in phishing, fake profiles, fake customer-care and investment scams. Punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine.

Reporting pathway: (1) immediately call the bank's fraud line and the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and request a transaction hold/freeze where possible; (2) file a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in), preserving transaction references (UTR/RRN), chat screenshots and account details; (3) approach the local police station or cyber cell with the printed complaint and evidence.

Compensation claims for unauthorized transactions additionally proceed through the bank's grievance redressal, the banking ombudsman framework of the RBI (verify current scheme details on the RBI portal), and the consumer commissions.

title: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Section 138 cheque dishonour
summary: Section 138 NI Act criminalizes dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds: after the bank's return memo, the holder must send a written demand notice, the drawer has 15 days to pay, failing which a criminal complaint lies before the Magistrate within one month (time-bound steps — verify the current provisos).
text:
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Section 138 (cheque bounce):

Where a cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by them for discharge of a debt or liability is returned by the bank unpaid — because of insufficiency of funds, or because it exceeds the arrangement — the drawer is punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or with fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

Statutory procedure (strictly time-bound; verify the current provisos at indiacode.nic.in):

1. The payee/holder must present the cheque within its validity period.
2. On dishonour, the bank issues a 'return memo'.
3. The holder must send a written demand notice to the drawer, ordinarily within 30 days of receiving the return-memo information of dishonour, calling upon the drawer to pay the cheque amount.
4. The drawer has 15 days from receipt of the notice to make payment.
5. If unpaid, the holder may file a criminal complaint before the Magistrate/Metropolitan Magistrate, ordinarily within one month of the expiry of the 15-day period (extension possible on sufficient cause).

Evidence essentials: the original dishonoured cheque, the bank's return memo, proof of dispatch and delivery of the demand notice, and material showing the debt/liability. A parallel civil suit for recovery is also possible.
